_readme: The supersede ledger — how BOSS tells a project that one of its OWN ways of doing something changed.
WHY THIS EXISTS: `boss sync` could add and modify, and its stated policy was 'nothing is removed'.
So a skill BOSS retired stayed in every project that ever synced, forever, alongside its replacement.
That inverts EVID-001's compose-and-subtract mandate at the exact moment it is meant to be honoured,
and it made DEC-003's fourth step ('if yes, BOSS does the migration') a promise the sync layer could
not keep. planSync can now detect an orphan on disk; this file is what lets it say WHY.
A removal without a reason is just a deletion. Every entry must be able to answer, to a founder who
never read the changelog: what went, what replaced it, why, and what they should do about it.
FIELDS
since       BOSS version the change landed in. sync only surfaces entries newer than the project's pin.
kind        skill | agent | hook
removed     the name as it appeared in the stage manifest (and on disk).
replacedBy  the name that takes over, or null when it was simply retired.
why         one honest founder-facing line. Not 'deprecated' — the actual reason.
migrate     what changes for the founder. Written to them, not about them.
RULES
- Append only. An entry describes a release that shipped; editing it rewrites history a project
may already have acted on.
- THE ONE EXCEPTION — COLLAPSING AN UNRELEASED CHAIN. If a replacement name is itself superseded
BEFORE the version carrying it was ever published, the earlier entry is rewritten to point at the
final name instead of chaining through a name no project could have installed. `mentor-business`
-> `mentor-money` -> `mentor-capital` became `mentor-business` -> `mentor-capital`, and no
`mentor-money` entry exists, because `mentor-money` lived one day inside an unpublished version.
THE TEST IS PUBLICATION, NOT INTENT: once a version ships to npm, its names are load-bearing and
every later change chains. Committed-but-unpublished is the only window this is allowed in.
WHY IT IS WORTH AN EXCEPTION: the ledger exists to tell a founder what to do, and routing them
through a name that never reached them is noise dressed as history. WHY IT IS NARROW: this rule
was written AFTER the edit it describes, which is exactly how a ledger stops being trustworthy.
A file that says 'append only' while being edited is worse than either policy stated honestly.
- Never remove something a founder EDITED without saying so — sync flags local edits by name first.
- Removal is never automatic. `boss sync --apply` reports it; `--remove` is the founder's consent.

supersedes.why: /pmf-check rendered the fit verdict and /retain diagnosed the decaying curve — from the same retention curve, behind the same n<10 gate, both rebasing past the same AI-tourist wave. Two skills for one question.
supersedes.migrate: `/health` does both: the verdict first, then where the curve dies. Your docs/pmf/ files stay where they are.

supersedes.why: Same reason as /pmf-check — you had to know whether you had a fit problem or a retention problem before picking the verb that would have told you.
supersedes.migrate: `/health` renders the verdict, then routes the diagnosis (activation → /onboard, engagement → the product + /roadmap, wallet → dunning via /money). Your docs/retain/ files stay where they are.

supersedes.why: /first-dollar took the first sale, /monetize ran the money after it — and each one's honest output, when it didn't apply, was 'go run the other one'.
supersedes.migrate: `/money` reads where you are and routes: no yes yet → /interview; a yes but no rail → the first-dollar path; paying customers → operating it. Your docs/first-dollar/ files stay where they are.

supersedes.why: Same pair. Splitting them made the founder identify their own revenue stage before choosing a skill.
supersedes.migrate: `/money` covers upgrades, dunning, price raises and expansion — pass the move as an argument (`/money dunning`) or let it ask. Your docs/monetize/ files stay where they are.

supersedes.why: BOSS shipped a ui/ux split to founders while running a SINGLE designer on itself — the project with the most opinionated interaction surface in the repo. The split's two descriptions ("what things look like" vs "what things do") had to be glossed every time they were named, and when the gloss is mandatory the name is not what's broken. One agent now owns both halves.
supersedes.migrate: `designer` replaces both, and arrives at MVP rather than V1. `/design-review` now runs it in two passes — the visual system first, then flows, states and content — so the review order you had is preserved. Your existing docs/design/ files are untouched.

supersedes.why: BOSS shipped TWO architects — one advisory (mentor-architect), one building (db-architect) — so the founder had to guess which to ask, and the one holding the best-evidenced security material in the whole product was the one you had to remember to open before writing a migration. That is exactly when you are least likely to. The chair became a gate.
supersedes.migrate: Ask `mentor-architect` the judgment questions it used to answer — one table or two, will this query scale, is this a one-way door, who can read a row. The mechanical half now fires on its own: `/spec` has a data-shape step that runs while the FEAT is still prose, and `schema-guard` (opt-in, `.claude/hooks/`) flags a CREATE TABLE whose migration has no row-level policy. The craft it carried was already extracted to `boss craft data-schema` in v0.142.0 — nothing was lost with the agent. Your docs/architecture/ files stay where they are.

supersedes.why: "Venture" reads as venture capital, and this is the cornerstone — the first and only mentor a project gets at Quickstart. For a founder who is deliberately building something right-sized, the very first advisor BOSS seats was named after the funding path they had already declined. Its job was never the raise; it is whether the idea is worth pursuing at all.
supersedes.migrate: `mentor-founder` is the same mentor with the same job — the whole arc, the riskiest assumption, the next real step, and the canvas conversation. It is the generalist; the others are the specialists (money, customers, hiring). Nothing about when it arrives or what it asks has changed.

supersedes.why: GTM is an acronym you have to already know. The cohorts BOSS most needs to reach — someone building their first product ever, or coming from a non-technical trade — cannot read it, and BOSS's own rule is assume intelligence, never assume knowledge. It is also mildly enterprise-shaped language for a job that is mostly "go find the first people who want this."
supersedes.migrate: `mentor-customers` is the same mentor: first users, channels, positioning, the actual first 100. If you have no customers yet, that is exactly when to open it — it is the mentor for getting them, not for managing them.

supersedes.why: "Business" covers everything, so it names nothing. This mentor has one subject — the model, the price, what someone will actually pay, and whether the unit economics hold — and it already sits beside `/money`, whose central step is the first price said out loud.
supersedes.migrate: `mentor-capital` is the same mentor, still at MVP, still the owner of `/money`'s first-price step. Same defaults, including "nobody has used this yet — go get a yes first."

supersedes.why: "Talent" is HR-department language for a question a founder asks in plain words: should I hire someone, and who first. It is also the vocabulary of the org this mentor exists to help you avoid building prematurely.
supersedes.migrate: `mentor-hiring` is the same mentor at Scale, still defaulting to *not yet* — first hires, contractors vs employees, what to keep, what to delegate, operating cadence.

supersedes.why: It collided by initialism with `pm`, and the two shipped side by side. A founder reading the roster saw two names that abbreviate identically and had to guess which owned sequencing. "Program manager" is also enterprise-org language for a job that is simply: what should I work on next, and is anything blocked.
supersedes.migrate: `planner` owns the same thing — the WHEN. What order, what is blocked, what can run in parallel, what this session should look like. `product-lead` still owns the WHAT.

supersedes.why: "Generalist" described BOSS's own roadmap — that this agent would later split into stack-specific coders — not anything the founder needed to know. BOSS's own prose had already voted: it says "a PM + a coder" and "pm + coder" in the places where it speaks plainly.
supersedes.migrate: `coder` is the same implementer, still stack-neutral until your first build decision pins a stack. When it does split later, the family stays legible: `coder-rust`, `coder-frontend`.

supersedes.why: An abbreviation that is ambiguous even to people who know it — product, project or program manager — and unreadable to the cohort BOSS's mode ladder exists to serve. It also collided by initialism with `program-manager`, which shipped alongside it.
supersedes.migrate: `product-lead` is the same agent, and it is what its own description always called it: the product lead. It decides what is worth building and why; `planner` decides when. Your `docs/ideas/` files are untouched; frontmatter that read `owner: pm` now reads `owner: product-lead`.

supersedes.why: BOSS calls itself a just-in-time incubator, and a real incubator does not staff a pricing specialist, a fundraising specialist and a pitch coach — one partner covers all three and gets deeper as the company does. Three chairs also meant a founder had to know which of them owned their question before they could ask it.
supersedes.migrate: `mentor-capital` holds this lens now and arrives at MVP rather than V1 — its remit widens at V1 instead of a new agent installing. It carries a hard "not yet" default on raising, and is required to surface its own money-vs-raise tension out loud rather than resolving it silently. Your docs/dossier/ files are untouched.
